references.text: Tells how Esau sold his birthright to Jacob for a meal, which follows directly after verse 29.
Esau discovers that Jacob has taken his blessing and refers back to the fact that Jacob had already taken his birthright (v.36).
Warns against immorality and godlessness, such as selling one's birthright for a single meal, as Esau did.
Both verses mark critical turning points where Esau returns from hunting just as Jacob's action (food or blessing) determines the inheritance rights.
